metaData.originalTitle: Agent Infra 实践复盘：Kimi 如何搭建 Agent 背后的 Database 服务
metaData.title: Agent Infra Practice Review: How Kimi Built the Database Service Behind Its Agent
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: PingCAP CTO Huang Dongxu reviews the practice of TiDB Cloud providing database support for Kimi K2.6 Agent website building service, revealing the core challenges and architectural choices of data infrastructure in the Agent era.
metaData.summary: This article, written by PingCAP co-founder and CTO Huang Dongxu, reviews the collaboration details of TiDB Cloud becoming the database provider for Kimi K2.6 Agent website building service. The article first points out that the core competition in the second half of the Agent era lies in stably and continuously delivering services, rather than model capabilities themselves. Kimi K2.6 targets general users, providing a full-process service from code generation to online hosting. Its core challenge lies in infrastructure costs under massive long-tail tenants. The article compares the architectural differences between traditional Serverless databases (such as Supabase, Neon) and TiDB Cloud: the former assigns real database instances to each Agent, with costs scaling linearly; the latter achieves extreme elasticity and cost control through a virtual database layer and underlying distributed KV storage. The article summarizes three core strategic decisions: minimizing the friction for Agents to use Infra tools (second-level creation), unifying the tech stack to improve the success rate of generated code, and achieving extremely low costs through architectural innovation. Finally, the author points out that "one agent, one sandbox, one storage, one database" has become a common paradigm for AI Agent teams.
metaData.featuredReason: PingCAP co-founder Huang Dongxu walks through what it took for TiDB Cloud to become the database backbone of Kimi K2.6 Agent. Kimi K2.6 lets anyone describe an app in plain text and get a working end-to-end deployment — the challenge isn't code generation, it's hosting cost across millions of dynamically created tiny sites. One Supabase instance per agent? Cost explosion. A single Postgres with multi-schema tenancy? Breaks past ten thousand tenants. TiDB Cloud's virtual database interface delivers tenant isolation, a unified stack, and instant elasticity at a per-tenant cost that actually works under subscription economics. The first real reference case for agent-native data infra.

mainPoints.point: The core competition in the second half of the Agent era is stably and continuously delivering services, not model capabilities.
mainPoints.explanation: When model capabilities converge, whether an Agent can stably run the generated results and continuously provide services to users becomes the key to commercial success. The case of Kimi K2.6 proves this point.

mainPoints.point: For Agent services targeting general users, the core challenge lies in infrastructure costs under massive long-tail tenants.
mainPoints.explanation: Kimi K2.6 targets users without a technical background, with a massive user base. Each user's generated site requires an independent database. If traditional solutions are adopted, costs will scale linearly with the number of tenants, making commercialization unfeasible.

mainPoints.point: TiDB Cloud achieves extreme elasticity and cost control through a virtual database layer and underlying distributed KV storage.
mainPoints.explanation: Unlike traditional Serverless databases that assign real instances to each tenant, TiDB Cloud introduces a virtual database interface, supported by a unified underlying distributed KV storage, achieving second-level creation, on-demand elasticity, hot/cold data separation, and significantly reducing costs.

mainPoints.point: Data infrastructure in the Agent era needs to simultaneously satisfy multi-tenant isolation, a unified tech stack, and instant elasticity.
mainPoints.explanation: The core reason Kimi chose TiDB is that it simultaneously excels at "per-tenant multi-tenant isolation, unified stack, and instant elasticity," rather than pursuing extreme performance on a single metric.

keyQuotes: The core competition in the second half of the Agent era is: whether the things and results delivered by the Agent can run stably in front of real users and be continuously delivered.

The competition for data Infra in the Agent-native era is quite different from the past 30 years. In the past, it was about single-point performance... but not now. Now it's about: when these four things happen simultaneously, who can provide the smoothest experience?

The core reason for choosing TiDB is not about achieving extreme performance on a single metric — but rather that when it comes to doing 'per-tenant multi-tenant isolation, unified stack, and instant elasticity' all at once, it is one of the few systems where each item is 'sufficient and convenient.'

A user might have 10 or even 100 Agents running around them, each requiring its own state and data... Including Kimi, some AI Agent teams operating as a business model have converged on the same paradigm: one agent, one sandbox, one storage, one database.
